articles.title: 2 Grand Canyon flooding victims photographed on hiking trip in days before deaths
articles.summary: John Giusti and Brent Rosenkranz, from Texas, posted selfies from the Grand Canyon before devastating flash flooding swept through the area on Saturday.
articles.body: The two victims whose remains were found after flash flooding swept through the Grand Canyon were seen photographed on the same trip prior to the deadly incident. The families of Texas chiropractor John Giusti, 46, and martial artist Brent Rosenkranz, 42, identified them as the two people whose bodies were recovered, according to Hannah Barricks, a liaison for the families. She told The Associated Press that a third friend, Timothy Smith, 53, went on the trip with them and remains missing as of late Monday. All three men had ties to Granbury, Texas, and their families said they planned "several days of hiking, camping, fishing and exploring together," the AP also reported. The men spoke to their families Thursday and found their campsite Friday at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, the three families said in a joint statement released earlier Monday through Barricks. The devastating flash flooding on Saturday, Aug. 29, happened along Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the Colorado River near Phantom Ranch. The area has a set of historic dormitories, a canteen and a campground that is a popular stopover for river rafters and people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other. GRAND CANYON WATER PIPELINE DAMAGED AGAIN AS FLOODING COMPLICATES REPAIRS Incident Cmdr. Dave Black said searchers used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed rescuing during the deluge. By sunset Saturday, 45 people were rescued, and 37 others were evacuated Sunday. Rangers referred to the park’s permit system and checked vehicle license plates to track the number of missing people. "As of right now, they have no reason to believe, from the tips we’ve been through so far, that there’s anybody besides the one" missing person, Black said during a news conference Monday evening. Hiker Daniel Evans told the AP that it rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel Campground area. Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go. He said he thought of Nepal and the massive floods and landslides that poured down mountain valleys last week. BELOVED TEXAS CHIROPRACTOR KILLED IN GRAND CANYON FLASH FLOOD "The entire time it was raining — the entire time I’m going through all this and packing — I’m just keeping my eyes upstream, just praying that a wall of water isn’t coming toward us," Evans said. Janet Giusti, the wife of John Giusti, wrote on a fundraising page that "John was living out a lifetime dream exploring the majesty of the Grand Canyon when tragedy struck." "Beyond his practice, he was a man of electric energy and boundless passion — an avid runner, an enthusiast of fast cars, and a massive fan of comic books and legendary heroes," she added. "Yet out of all the titles he carried, his absolute favorite was being a devoted father to his three beautiful girls." Rosenkranz had posted selfies from the Grand Canyon before the flooding, tagging Giusti and sharing his excitement about the grueling adventure ahead. "Just arrived at the Grand Canyon. Will be hiking over 31 miles next four days with vertical change of over a mile," Rosenkranz wrote. "Carrying a 40 lb backpack. This should be an adventure!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tina Newberry, whose daughter co-owns the ATA Glen Rose martial arts location, said Giusti had been exploring the canyon with fellow "ATA fathers" Rosenkranz and Smith when disaster struck. Fox News Digital’s Stepheny Price and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
articles.summary: The UK says Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".
articles.body:
Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.

The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

Trump's remarks were labelled "nonsense" by Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, as she asked the UK government to issue an official response in the House of Commons.

Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran replied: "The UK has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

"They are and will always remain a British overseas territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders.

"The UK is steadfast in our support for the islanders' rights of self-determination."

Kumaran said she had seen Trump's comments, adding: "Our position remains unchanged."

In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.

The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

Reports of this proposal have re-emerged in recent days in relation to defence spending.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will honour a commitment made by predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to devote 3.5% of UK gross domestic product (GDP) on core defence spending by 2035.

On Tuesday, Chancellor John Healey told The Times he would "set out a clear path" to meeting that Nato pledge at the next government spending review, expected in the spring of next year.

He added that this would also include a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP.

Healey resigned as defence secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government following a row over military spending.

His resignation letter in June expressed his frustration that the government had no clear timetable to hit the 3% spending target, which he believed should happen by 2030.

The UK government has also faced questions over whether it will continue with a deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.

It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.

Kumaran told MPs on Tuesday that "maintaining long-term operational control and security of the base remains a top priority and is the entire basis for the UK-Mauritius agreement."

The minister also said funding for the treaty would be provided for "within the existing spending review settlements" for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the Ministry of Defence.

Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge criticised the remarks and said the deal "belongs on the ash heap of history".

He said in a statement: "Burnham should show some backbone and break with this terrible legacy of the Starmer years by ditching his crazy Chagos deal once and for all, and spending the savings on our armed forces."

In the Commons, Conservative shadow Foreign Office minister Wendy Morton noted Sir Keir's administration acknowledged in April that the Chagos treaty had become "impossible to agree at political level" and asked what had changed.

Kumaran said the Burnham government would "continue to work with the US and Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK's best interests and protects our national security".

articles.title: Iran urges US to honour commitments under MoU
articles.summary: Tehran calls for Washington to respect terms of MoU after attacks send tensions soaring in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
President Masoud Pezeshkian says Iran is ready to return to the terms of an interim agreement reached with the United States in June, which was aimed at ending the war, if Washington also does the same.

Pezeshkian made the comments at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Tuesday, a day after the first ⁠exchange of fire between the US and Iran in nearly a month. US forces attacked Larak Island, leading to Iran’s retaliation, with attacks on two airbases used by them in Jordan.

“I am stating clearly ‌that if the US returns to its commitments under the memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said, according to IRNA, the Iranian state news agency.

In mid-June, Iran and the US signed a Pakistan- and Qatar-brokered MoU which provided for a ceasefire extension, initiating a 60-day period for negotiations aimed at ending the war, which started with US and Israeli ⁠strikes on Tehran on February 28.

Under the terms of the MoU, Iran agreed to clear the Strait of Hormuz of mines and allow ships to pass during the period, and the US agreed to end its naval blockade, lift sanctions, issue waivers for Iranian oil exports and begin work on a reconstruction package for Iran.

However, the ceasefire collapsed within weeks, with the US and Iran again exchanging strikes amid Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the strait. Subsequently, the MoU lapsed last month.

“America’s commitment to the document signed by the president of that country lasted less than two weeks, and that country’s excessive demands and reneging on its commitments began, which still continues,” Pezeshkian said, according to IRNA.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US “broke its promises” under the MoU.

Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Tuesday the “sincere implementation” of the MoU signed in June remains the “only way forward” to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

“The return of escalation in the region is in no one’s interest,” Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told a news conference in Doha.

Al-Ansari said Qatar is working with all partners to reach a peaceful solution and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Officials from Pakistan, Qatar and Oman, among others, had travelled to Tehran for talks last week in a renewed diplomatic push before the latest exchange of attacks between Iran and the US.

articles.title: Why China will not comply with US sanctions on Iran
articles.summary: Beijing will not comply with US measures because it can and because it’s in its interest not to.
articles.body:
On August 31, the leaders of China, Russia and India met in Bishkek for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was also in attendance.

The final declaration of the summit issued on September 1 called for the creation of a new development bank, which in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s words would have “maximum independence from the financial systems of the states which weaponize economic tools in order to obtain unilateral advantages in international affairs”

The summit was held just a week after the United States announced the latest package of sanctions against Iran, which instead of isolation, enjoyed a warm welcome in Bishkek.

As the SCO gathering demonstrated, Washington is already facing major difficulties in ensuring international compliance with its sanctions.

Perhaps its biggest challenger is China. Beijing is once again standing by Iran – not out of moral or ideological motivations, but because it can and because it is in its interest.

By purchasing 90 percent of Iranian oil exports, China has single-handedly kept the Iranian economy afloat – all while evading the US sanctions through a sophisticated network of “dark fleets” (ships used to obfuscate the Iranian origin of their cargo) and “teapot” refineries (private refineries so dubbed for their relatively modest size).

In response to Washington’s “with us or against us” ultimatum on the sanctions, the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said that “China will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests”. Having fought several trade wars with the US to a standstill, China has developed a high tolerance for US-inflicted economic pain – and an equally low tolerance for being pushed around.

For Beijing, foreign interference in bilateral trade relations with a third country is not acceptable. More importantly, it views Washington’s threat as toothless – and for good reason.

China is well insulated from the US’ Iran-related secondary sanctions. Chinese banks and companies that do business with Iran often do so exclusively, settling transactions in renminbi or through barter – making them effectively immune to US extraterritorial jurisdiction.

Meanwhile, the handful of Chinese companies that still settle transactions in US dollars are hidden beneath layers of shell companies that can be discarded at little to no cost. This forces Washington into an endless game of regulatory whack-a-mole, in which each entity successfully eliminated is quickly replaced by another.

Washington could, of course, sanction major Chinese banks and companies that have no ties with Iran – using them as a bargaining chip to pressure Beijing to rein in those that do. Doing so, however, would invite Beijing to retaliate in kind. With the US economy already strained by the war with Iran and the midterms just around the corner, picking a fight with China is the last thing the US needs.

Toothless US sanctions aside, China has another motive for standing by Iran’s side: its defeat could be costly for Chinese geopolitical and economic interests.

From Beijing’s perspective, should Iran lose, the entire Middle East would gravitate back into the US orbit. Regional countries currently exploring alternative security partners would have little choice but to seek refuge once more under the US security umbrella.

Such a shift would not only deal a heavy blow to China’s growing influence in the region but also complicate future cooperation on advanced technologies, including 5G, artificial intelligence, and defence.

Worse still, China’s energy interests could be threatened. The country sources 40 percent of its oil imports from the Gulf, with Iran accounting for 10 percent. With such a significant chunk of oil imports originating from countries under US influence, China’s economic lifeline would effectively lie in US hands.

A victory in Iran would also embolden Washington to continue its pursuit of regime-change in other countries that have close ties with Beijing.

This would make it increasingly difficult for China to protect its interests overseas, as was the case when Panama seized two Chinese-operated ports under US pressure.

That said, China does not see itself in a tight alliance with Iran – hence its reluctance to ramp up support.

It is worried that a total victory for Iran would enable its regional hegemony, driving yet another wedge in the already strained relationship with the Gulf states, and further undermining years of Chinese diplomatic efforts aimed at bridging that divide.

Therefore, Beijing is maintaining a calibrated distance from Tehran – not too hot, not too cold, but just right. The fact that Pezeshkian is yet to be invited to Beijing makes it clear the Chinese authorities are not eager for a tight embrace.

This was apparent at the SCO summit as well. The Chinese leader met with his Russian and Indian counterparts, but did not have a formal meeting with Pezeshkian. There were formal consultations at the level of foreign ministers.

The message is subtle yet unmistakable: Though Beijing values the relationship, it is keeping its distance.

When considering the China-Iran relationship, it’s important to remember that relations with the US, although often fraught by rivalry, are very important for Beijing.

Resetting of China-US relations takes priority, which is why two high-level summits are taking place this year: The first one was US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and the second is Xi’s trip to Washington later this month.

During Trump’s visit to China this May, he and Xi announced that the two countries had agreed on building a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability” – one where cooperation takes centre stage, competition is kept within bounds and never descends into zero-sum games, and war is to be avoided at all cost.

In this context, providing too much support to Iran would be counterproductive – which is why Beijing has stayed out of the war and has pledged not to arm Iran. This is clearly appreciated in Washington. In June, Trump thanked China publicly for remaining “totally neutral”.

At the same time the Trump administration is well aware of China’s economic interest in Iran and was likely not surprised to hear its position on the new sanctions.

The only way out of this self-inflicted predicament is for Washington to shed its hegemonic mindset and return to the negotiating table – anything less will only prolong the misery – both for itself, and for the world at large.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: SCO slams attacks, sanctions on Iran: Key takeaways from Bishkek summit
articles.summary: The SCO started in 1996 and accounts for 43 percent of the world’s population and 23 percent of the global economy.
articles.body:
Leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) have signed a joint statement condemning the US and Israel’s war on Iran and Western sanctions on some of their members, after a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek.

The joint statement, called the “Bishkek Declaration”, was signed by Chinese President Xi Jinping, his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, among other leaders of SCO member nations. The SCO consists of Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and the Kyrgyz Republic.

SCO condemns attacks and sanctions on Iran, attacks on Palestine

The SCO condemned “military strikes on the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which have resulted in numerous civilian casualties and significant damage to the country’s economy”.

They said that the US-Israel attacks on Iran “violate the principles and norms of international law and the UN Charter and create serious risks to international peace, security and stability”.

“Member States express their sincere condolences to the people and Government of the Islamic Republic of Iran on the tragic death of Supreme Leader Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and to the families of the victims,” the declaration added.

SCO members also reaffirmed “their support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Islamic Republic of Iran and advocate a resolution to the conflict solely through political and diplomatic means.”

The declaration also mentioned that Israel’s attacks on Palestine had destabilised West Asia.

“Member States note that the only possible way to ensure peace and stability in the Middle East is a comprehensive and just settlement of the Palestinian question,” the declaration said.

Without specifying US sanctions on Iran and on countries doing business with Iran, and Western sanctions on Russia due to its war on Ukraine, SCO members also said in their declaration that they are opposed to any “unilateral coercive measures” that go against the rules of the UN and World Trade Organization and could have a “negative impact on the global economy.”

The grouping’s leaders also backed Iran’s rights as a member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).

Apart from the US, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France, other NPT signatories cannot build nuclear weapons. But they have the right to a peaceful nuclear programme. They can build civilian nuclear reactors, and use nuclear technology for research and medicine.

Though the US has long accused Iran of secretly harbouring the ambition of building nuclear bombs, Iran has consistently denied those accusations, insisting it is only interested in a peaceful programme. It is on that basis that the US and Iran struck their 2015 nuclear deal – Iran agreed to limit uranium enrichment to 3 percent, which is enough for civilian reactors, but well below the levels of enrichment needed for a nuclear bomb.

But the US under President Donald Trump first bombed Iran in 2025 and then – alongside Israel – launched the war on Iran in February 2026, arguing that the military action was aimed at stopping Iran from building a nuclear weapon.

Then, Trump insisted that Iran would need to completely surrender its nuclear programme – including domestic uranium enrichment. Iran has rejected that demand, pointing out that it would mean foregoing its NPT rights.

The SCO on Tuesday upheld the position of Iran, itself an SCO member.

SCO members emphasised “their inalienable right” to develop research, produce and use atomic energy “for peaceful purposes and to pursue equitable, sustainable, and mutually beneficial international cooperation in this area without discrimination.” They said that any measures which restrict this right are “contrary to international law.”

Economic cooperation was also a key topic SCO members discussed as the US and Israel’s war on Iran continues to hobble trade through key maritime routes, such as the Strait of Hormuz, which in turn has upended global supply chains, the energy market and financial markets.

In their Bishkek declaration, members said they will “support and strengthen an open, transparent, fair, inclusive, and non-discriminatory multilateral trading system based on generally accepted international principles and rules that promotes global economic development, ensures fair market access, and ensures special and differential treatment for developing countries.”

They also said they would implement “the SCO Economic Development Strategy for the period up to 2030” in order to deepen economic cooperation and said they would continue “to develop practical dialogue to strengthen financial cooperation.”

Amid the global energy market’s paralysis due to the war in Iran, SCO members also said they “support the expansion of inclusive and mutually beneficial cooperation in energy” and agreed to implement “the SCO Member States’ Energy Cooperation Strategy to 2030.”

India and Pakistan faced off – as they have previously at multilateral platforms, including the United Nations – on the issue of “terrorism” that they each accuse the other of sponsoring.

India has since the late 1980s accused Pakistan of arming, financing and sheltering armed groups to feed a rebellion in Indian-administered Kashmir. Since the 1990s, New Delhi has also accused Pakistan of backing “terrorist” acts across India, including the Mumbai attacks of 2008.

Pakistan has rejected accusations of a systematic strategy of using armed groups against India, but has conceded specific instances where fighters who attacked India were proven to be Pakistani. In recent years, it too has accused India of backing armed groups that have targeted Pakistan – a charge New Delhi rejects.

On Tuesday, India’s Modi described terrorism as a “grave challenge to all of humanity”, and asked countries to steer clear of “double standards” on the issue.

“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens. We must speak with one voice and make it clear that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue,” Modi said. “We must send a strong message to countries that use terrorism as an instrument of policy and provide safe haven and support to terrorists that terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.”

Observers widely interpreted his comments as aimed at Pakistan.

Pakistan’s Sharif, however, himself insisted that Islamabad was a victim of terrorism.

“Recalling Pakistan’s immense sacrifices in the fight against terrorism, I reiterated that terrorism must be condemned in all its forms and manifestations,” he said.

In the Bishkek declaration, SCO leaders committed to combat “terrorism, separatism, and extremism”.

“Member States strongly condemn terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, emphasise that ‘double standards’ in the fight against terrorism are unacceptable, and call on the international community to combat terrorism, including the cross-border movement of terrorists,” SCO leaders added.

articles.title: 'Can even become US president': Palaniswami takes dig at TN CM Vijay's 'PM ambitions'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: As TVK leaders project Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay as the next Prime Minister, AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: As TVK leaders project Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay as the next Prime Minister, AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami on Tuesday took a sharp jibe at TVK chief, saying that he could "even become the President of the United States."Mocking Vijay's extensive public relations campaigns and penchant for chartered flights, EPS said, "He could even become the President of America. There is nothing wrong with it, it is his wish.""They are running the government by putting out 'reels' here; that won't work there," he added.He also labelled Vijay as a "costly chief minister" and contrasted the current administration's expenditure with that of former chief minister J Jayalalithaa."During Amma's tenure, projects were inaugurated via video conferencing to cut costs," Palaniswami said.This comes amid a recent push by TVK leaders to project Vijay as a potential contender for the PM's post. TVK PWD minister Aadhav Arjuna had earlier said the country's top constitutional office should be held by a leader from Tamil Nadu.TVK leaders, including KA Sengottaiyan and D Sarathkumar, have compared Vijay with former Tamil Nadu chief ministers MGR and Jayalalithaa, claiming he would not only rule Tamil Nadu but also lead the country in the future.TVK MLA Kallanai, who organised an event marking the party's 100 days in office, said people had immense faith in Vijay's leadership. He expressed confidence that Vijay would eventually lead the country and hoist the national flag at the Red Fort as a representative of the Tamil people, news agency PTI reported.Congress MP Karti Chidambaram said that while party workers may have deep admiration for their leader, national leadership ultimately depends on securing the numbers required to form a government."I fully accept that they have great love, affection, expectation, and admiration for their party leadership. This is their party. What they say within their party makes no difference to the public discourse. In public discourse, what you should ask about is policy and the law. Their wishes within a party make no difference to me," Chidambaram told reporters, according to ANI.He said every political party has its own ambitions and aspirations, but any prime ministerial aspirant must ultimately have the numbers to command a majority in Lok Sabha."Every party has dreams, ambitions, and desires. There are 543 constituencies," Chidambaram said.The issue has gained further attention after a private media survey placed Vijay among the preferred candidates for PM in 2029, behind PM Narendra Modi and Rahul Gandhi.The TVK government was formed after the 2026 Tamil Nadu assembly elections, when the party emerged as the largest force and formed the government with support from VCK, IUML, Congress, CPI and CPM.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ICE arrests 50,000 people in August, continuing record pace
articles.summary: ICE is in the midst of a nationwide arrest surge that is not as visible as aggressive enforcement efforts from earlier in 2026.
articles.body: ICE officers and agents arrested roughly 50,000 people in August, according to a senior Department of Homeland Security official familiar with the preliminary arrest data. That number is on par with July’s number, which was the highest single monthly arrest total during the second Trump administration. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is in the midst of a nationwide arrest surge that is not as visible as aggressive enforcement efforts from earlier in the year when Border Patrol was going city by city culminating in the shooting deaths of two American citizens in Minneapolis. Arrests fell sharply in February and March but then began to rise in May. June and July both had record ICE arrests according to ICE arrest data. In June, the Republican-controlled House narrowly passed a roughly $70 billion package to fund ICE and the Border Patrol through the end of President Donald Trump’s term. The sweeping tax and spending bill made ICE the wealthiest law enforcement agency in American history. That pool of money has been used to purchase new “turnkey” facilities for immigration detention, as well as the planned purchase of immigration enforcement tools such as electric gloves and robot dogs. ICE has also moved forward with some additional detention capacity including the recent signing of a new contractor to manage the operations of a new ICE warehouse in San Antonio, Texas, for $17 million, according to government contracting records.

articles.title: Gary, Indiana, can’t blame racism for every failure exposed by its catastrophic blackout
articles.summary: A derecho with 99 mph winds left Gary, Indiana, in darkness for weeks, but Project H.O.O.D. says blaming systemic racism won't rebuild the city.
articles.body: Gary, Indiana, sits on the southern shore of Lake Michigan not too far from where I am on the South Side of Chicago. I know that city well and my Project H.O.O.D. has done many events and good works there. The one thing everybody knows about Gary is that it is the birthplace of Michael Jackson, a place where one of the biggest stars the world has ever known was forged. In the years before Jackson was born, Blacks moved to Gary from the South to work in the steel mills and many made good livings. But today, Gary sits in the middle of the Rust Belt, and it faces high poverty, widespread vacancy and a long population decline. Its population fell from more than 80,000 in 2010 to an estimated 67,289 in 2025. Gary is one of those places where the streak of bad luck never seems to run out. I say this with a heavy heart because I know that many people there are good people and they’re trying their best to make some kind of fortune out of their city’s misfortunes. What no one could have predicted is what hit them next — literally. THE MACHINES THAT KEEP AMERICA ALIVE ARE FAILING. WE FORGOT HOW TO REPLACE THEM The weather people on TV call it a derecho. Unlike a tornado that spins in a circle, a derecho consists of winds running straight through with great force. On Aug. 11, a derecho swept through Northwest Indiana, bringing widespread straight-line winds of 70 to more than 100 mph. A 99 mph wind gust was recorded at Gary/Chicago International Airport. Those gusts were comparable to the winds associated with a Category 2 hurricane. For nearly two weeks, thousands of Gary residents remained without power. The suffering on the ground was terrible. While many of the nearby towns and suburbs felt the derecho, Gary was among the communities hardest hit. I heard from my contacts there that trees that stood for generations had been uprooted and fallen into power lines. The poles holding these lines snapped. The storm brought down trees and power lines across Gary, causing widespread outages. More than 20,000 Gary customers were affected at one point. Within a few hours, it appeared as if nearly everybody in Gary lost power. The city that once powered America’s steel industry was now sitting in darkness. HURRICANE KATRINA TAUGHT ME HOW TO PREPARE FOR ANY STORM For nearly two weeks, thousands of Gary residents remained without power. The suffering on the ground was terrible. There was no air conditioning to combat the sweltering heat. Senior citizens who needed breathing machines had to do without. Parents had to take what food they had in their warm fridges and save what they could by cooking the meats at the nearby parks. Some families who were fortunate enough to have generators were soon reporting them stolen. People couldn’t charge their phones and businesses couldn’t stay open. Life in Gary came to a literal standstill. NIPSCO now says it has restored power to 99% of affected customers, though some residents still need repairs to privately owned equipment before they can safely reconnect. FORGET POLITICS. THIS IS WHAT I FOUND HELPING VENEZUELAN QUAKE VICTIMS In the nearby towns, the lights began to flicker back on and the people in Gary thought they would soon be next. But the days went by and there was still no power. My Project H.O.O.D. team drove into Gary along with many other nonprofits and churches, and we lent a helping hand wherever needed. After the derecho hit, we got calls and texts from our friends in Gary and we knew we had to help in any way possible. We brought people produce, hot meals and the basic necessities such as soap, shampoo, toothpaste and the like. Just because the infrastructure failed the people of Gary, it doesn’t mean that we humans can’t come together and help one another. DIVINE PURPOSE HELPED BRING CHICAGO’S MOST-DANGEROUS BLOCK BACK TO LIFE While in the streets, I started to hear the word that the reason for the lack of power was racism. Gary is a Black city and some folks there felt they were deliberately being left behind. People said, "Why isn’t our power on? Why do all the White folks have their power and we don’t?" As time passed, these mutterings grew angrier and expletive-laden. I understand their frustrations and I understand the human need to reach for explanations, but feelings are not facts. When a derecho exposes failures on a catastrophic level, the temptation is to shout ‘systemic racism’ and wait for someone else to fix it. This mindset has kept too many of our communities in the dark long before any derecho arrived. Gary was in the direct line of fire and the utility company’s damage assessments show that the city suffered an unbelievable amount of damage. The utility said the derecho caused historic damage across Northwest Indiana, including roughly 300 damaged distribution poles and 44 damaged transmission poles. The scale of that damage complicated restoration in Gary and other hard-hit communities. What I have read shows that the process to restore power must follow a standard order: major lines are targeted first so the greatest number of customers can be restored safely and efficiently. This is not bigotry. This is engineering. Blaming race here does not turn the lights back on. It only gives everyone an easy excuse to avoid the harder work. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION And the harder work has been avoided for too long. The outage has prompted serious questions about whether tree-trimming and grid preparedness were adequate. A proposed lawsuit makes those allegations, while NIPSCO disputes them and says it has increased vegetation-management spending. All around, the infrastructure weakens with every passing year and no one wants to invest. The leaders seem to be in the mode of managing decline instead of demanding excellence. And so, when the derecho exposes these failures on a catastrophic level, the temptation is to shout "systemic racism" and wait for someone else to fix it. This mindset has kept too many of our communities in the dark long before any derecho arrived. What the aftermath of the derecho revealed was a resilient, compassionate and strong community. Residents have been caring for their neighbors and sharing what little they have. The churches and volunteers came together to hand out meals. Outsiders drove into Gary in trucks and even semitrucks full of food. My team will be back, and we plan to open our second Project H.O.O.D. location in Gary. We will provide workforce development programs, mentorship for the youth, violence prevention, reentry rehabilitation for the formerly incarcerated and more. Why all this energy now? There wasn’t much of this energy before the derecho hit, and that is why we have to ask, "Why now? Are we going to let this energy go to waste?" I hope not because this is the kind of energy that builds cities. That builds neighborhoods. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What the derecho revealed is that we have the strength, manpower and will to make our lives better. All this talk about systemic racism will only keep us down. Perhaps that is the lesson here and the one that the people of Gary need to hold onto if they want to climb out of this hole. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM PASTOR COREY BROOKS

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy jurors are deadlocked, judge sends them back for more deliberations
articles.summary: The jury in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial told the judge Tuesday morning that it was unable to come to a unanimous decision at the start of a fourth day of deliberations.
articles.body: The jury in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial told the judge Tuesday morning that it was unable to come to a unanimous decision at the start of a fourth day of deliberations. Judge William Sullivan instructed the jurors to go back and continue deliberations. “I know that this was a long trial,” he said. “I know there were over 80 witnesses, over 300 exhibits. But because of that, I’m going to ask you to go back out, keeping in mind all the instructions that I gave you. To go out and to continue your deliberations at this time.” Clancy, wearing a beige sweater, did not appear to show any emotion. Her parents and sister were also present in the courtroom. The prosecution and Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, did not object. Under Massachusetts law, Sullivan can encourage the jury to go back to the jury room, but not more than twice unless the jury consents to it. If the jury still cannot reach a unanimous verdict, the judge can declare a mistrial. Earlier Tuesday, Reddington had said that he would “absolutely” go to trial again if the verdict ends in a hung jury. “Maybe today’s the day; we’ll see. I don’t know,” said Reddington, who is representing Clancy in a murder trial that will determine if she is criminally liable in the killings of her three young children. The attorney said he has “really strong faith” in the jury, noting that members showed attentiveness throughout the five-week trial. When asked by a reporter what a hung jury would mean, Reddington responded: “Try it again.” “Would you do the trial again if there’s a hung jury?” another reporter asked. “Absolutely,” Reddington said. Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor with expertise in criminal and mental disability law, said generally “the longer a jury remains deadlocked, the greater the possibility of a hung jury.” “Deadlocks are not uncommon in complex, emotionally charged cases, particularly when jurors must evaluate extensive evidence and conflicting expert testimony,” Cucolo said. But if the jury continues to be at loggerheads, the judge could give the panel a supplemental instruction commonly referred to as a “dynamite charge,” Cucolo said. In Massachusetts, this instruction is known as a “Tuey Rodriguez charge,” or simply a “Rodriguez charge.” “The purpose is to encourage jurors to reexamine their positions, consider differing viewpoints, and work toward a unanimous verdict without abandoning their sincerely held convictions,” Cucolo said. Asked what might be deadlocking this jury, Cucolo said “it is difficult to know from the outside.” “However, given the issues presented in this case, the disagreement may stem from differing views of the psychiatric and medical evidence, as well as questions concerning intent, premeditation, and criminal responsibility,” she said. The 12-person jury made up of nine women and three men began deliberating Thursday afternoon. The jury had one question Friday when it asked the judge to review pill bottles and a knife that had been entered into evidence. The jury is weighing whether to convict Clancy of first-degree murder after she was accused of using exercise bands to strangle her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — in the basement of their Duxbury home in January 2023. Her then-husband, who was running errands at the time, found her outside underneath a second-story window following a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed from the waist down. Clancy’s attorney has argued that she was in a state of postpartum psychosis and heard a voice at the time of the killings. According to Clancy’s legal team, she had previously sought help for mental health issues. Prosecutors, however, said she was not in psychosis and planned the murders ahead of time. The jury also has the option to convict her of lesser charges, including second-degree murder and manslaughter, or absolve her of the crime or deem her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. If the jury finds her not criminally responsible, that means that jurors believe she could not control her actions because she was in psychosis. The case has garnered national headlines, fueling social media chatter and podcasts for weeks as spectators debate postpartum mental illness and the gaps in maternal healthcare raised during the trial. Supporters of Clancy, often dressed in pink, have gathered outside the Plymouth, Massachusetts, courthouse and sat in the gallery throughout the trial.

articles.title: In 1943, two Jewish refugees fleeing the Nazis bought a crumbling Los Angeles mansion for $9,000; 83 years later, after the Palisades Fire forced it shut, Villa Aurora has reopened
articles.summary: US News: In 1943, German Jewish writer Lion Feuchtwanger and his wife, Marta, bought a crumbling mansion in Pacific Palisades, Los Angels, for $9,000. The coup.
articles.body: In 1943, German Jewish writer Lion Feuchtwanger and his wife, Marta, bought a crumbling mansion in Pacific Palisades, Los Angels, for $9,000. The couple who had fled Nazi persecution, turned the house into a gathering place for artists, writers and intellectuals.The property, now known as Villa Aurora, was built in 1927 as a Spanish Revival model home. According to Los Angeles Times, when the Feuchtwangers bought it, its remote location, wartime gas shortages and poor condition had brought its price down.The couple had first fled Germany in 1933 and taken refuge in Southern France. They later arrived in Los Angeles, where a growing community of European artists and intellectuals had settled. Their new home soon became part of that community and was described as a cultural hub known as 'Weimar by the sea'.More than eight decades later, January 2025 Palisades Fire had forced it to close. On Sunday, Villa Aurora reopened to the public after restoration work was carried out.Feuchtwangers' time at the villaFrom 1943 until his death in 1958, Feuchtwanger worked at the villa and wrote some of his important works there, including a novel based on Spanish painter Francisco Goya.Marta Feuchtwanger also became a well-known figure in Los Angeles’ cultural circles. The couple hosted readings and tea parties attended by writers, composers, filmmakers and other prominent figures. Guests included Thomas and Heinrich Mann, Aldous Huxley, Bertolt Brecht, Charlie Chaplin and composer Hanns Eisler.The villa’s history was closely linked to the experience of German and Jewish exiles who had left Europe because of Nazi persecution. Los Angeles became home to several major figures from European cultural life, including Fritz Lang, Otto Preminger, Billy Wilder, Arnold Schoenberg and Erich Wolfgang Korngold.The Feuchtwangers remained at the property for decades. Marta lived there until her death in 1987 at the age of 96. Under her husband’s will, the property and its 32,000-volume library of rare books went to the University of Southern California.That transfer, however, put the future of the house in doubt. The deteriorating building and the Feuchtwanger archive needed millions of dollars in upkeep, and USC considered selling the property.A Berlin-based organisation called Friends of Villa Aurora eventually raised $1.9 million and bought the property from USC in 1989. A three-year renovation costing $1.6 million followed, with funding from the Berlin Lottery Foundation. Villa Aurora officially reopened in December 1995.An artist residencyAfter its 1995 reopening, Villa Aurora became an international artist residency. It provided a place for European writers, composers, filmmakers and visual artists to live and work while connecting with the Los Angeles cultural community.The residency also continued the house’s original role as a place for cultural exchange. Artists shared their work through screenings, exhibitions, readings and panel discussions.The programme later became a major part of Villa Aurora’s work. Artists from across Europe could apply to spend time at the residence and develop their projects. The organisation also supported writers facing persecution through the Feuchtwanger Fellowship.The villa’s also developed links with museums, universities, Jewish organisations and other cultural institutions. Its programmes included exhibitions, film screenings, lectures and discussions about exile and the Holocaust.Villa Aurora director Joachim Bernauer said in a Los Angeles Times report, “We have a national obligation to preserve a place like this. Here, we experience 20th century German history, with its light side- the intellectual richness and its dark one- the Holocaust. It’s important that we remember what went on.”The Palisades fire That work was interrupted by the January 2025 Palisades Fire, which severely affected the surrounding Pacific Palisades area and forced Villa Aurora to shut its doors.The fellowship programme continued away from the property while restoration work took place. According to Villa Aurora, the work included removing smoke damage from the building’s interior, carrying out toxicological and geotechnical assessments, conducting structural inspections and restoring the fire-damaged garden. The restoration was also supported by Germany’s Federal Foreign Office.“The extraordinary support and solidarity we experienced in both Germany and the United States carried us through the difficult months following the fires. We are excited to reopen the house to the public and to fully resume our work as a transatlantic cultural institution centered around the fellowship program,” Villa Aurora Director Claudia Gordon said earlier this month. The fellows are expected to return to the residence in October.Villa Aurora opens its doors againVilla Aurora reopened to the public on Sunday with a free open house at the property at 520 Paseo Miramar in Pacific Palisades.The event included stations across the house and grounds highlighting Villa Aurora’s programmes and cultural partnerships, My News LA reported. It also featured the return of two historic objects that had been removed from the property for safekeeping after the fire.One was a 1932 portrait of Marta Feuchtwanger. The other was an 18th-century Ashkenazic parchment scroll of the Megillat Esther, or Book of Esther.Villa Aurora has hosted nearly 500 writers, composers, visual artists and filmmakers since reopening as an international artist residency in 1995.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Is Trump wooing Russia again – and why?
articles.summary: CIA chief’s Moscow visit and Russian finance minister attending a G20 meeting in the US signal renewed dialogue.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration appears to be taking steps to increase contact with key figures in Moscow, even as Russia’s war in Ukraine continues and US-backed peace efforts remain stalled.

The latest signs that the US wants to step up relations include a rare visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe and the surprise appearance of Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a Group of 20 meeting hosted by the US on Monday.

However, this contact does not necessarily amount to a restoration of US-Russian relations, analysts said.

Washington continues to back sanctions against Moscow while it wages war on Ukraine and major differences over territory remain unresolved.

So what were these latest contacts about, and are US-Russian relations on the up?

What US-Russian contact has there been in recent days?

The most significant meeting recently was Ratcliffe’s visit last week to Moscow, where he held talks with Russian intelligence officials.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said President Vladimir Putin was informed about the discussions but did not personally meet Ratcliffe.

Trump described the visit as “semiroutine” and said it was connected to efforts to end the war in Ukraine . US media reported that Ratcliffe also raised concerns about a possible Russian attack on NATO members and Russia’s relationship with Iran.

Trump, who claimed he would end the Ukraine war within “24 hours” of starting his second presidential term in January 2025 but has since failed to broker an agreement, has generally sought to play down tensions between Washington and Moscow. After Ratcliffe’s visit, he said the CIA director had had “good talks” with Putin. “He’s not going to be attacking a NATO territory,” Trump said.

Despite that, Russia has warned recently that the United Kingdom could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory. “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which ⁠it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement in mid-August. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”

Separately, Siluanov made a surprise appearance at a G20 finance ministers meeting in the US state of North Carolina for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Siluanov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting.

According to the Reuters news agency, Bessent made clear there would be no financial agreements or economic relief for Russia until the war ends.

What is the latest on US-Russian talks on Ukraine?

Hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak as neither side is willing to concede territory to the other. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks this year broke down chiefly over Moscow’s territorial demands. Moscow has demanded that Kyiv give up territory in eastern Ukraine while Kyiv has refused to surrender any land it still controls.

Last week, Ukraine’s top presidential adviser, Kyrylo Budanov, said talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the US could be happening “very soon”.

On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had held “detailed and constructive” discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about a possible visit to Ukraine and efforts to advance the peace process.

In the meantime, the deadlock continues. Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange attacks, targeting each other’s energy infrastructure and fighting intense battles in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region.

On Tuesday, Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured many more in Kyiv and surrounding areas, local authorities said. It was the sixth consecutive day of intense strikes on the capital.

Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelenskyy’s sanctions commissioner, told Reuters on Monday that he is due in the US capital on Tuesday on a trip that will include meetings with lawmakers.

Are US-Russian relations improving? If so, what does that mean?

The restoration of high-level contacts between the US and Russia began earlier in Trump’s second term.

In February, Washington and Moscow agreed to re-establish high-level military-to-military talks, which were suspended just before the Russian war on Ukraine began.

After the latest contacts, Keir Giles, an associate fellow of the Russia and Eurasia Programme at the think tank Chatham House, said evidence that “relations are being normalised between Washington and Moscow should deepen the sense of alarm”.

“The US treating Russia as a partner not an adversary is a fundamental problem for all those countries that are under direct threat from Moscow – not just Ukraine but America’s European allies too,” Giles told Al Jazeera.

Insiders have also warned that a rapprochement with Trump could further embolden Russia against NATO. In August after Moscow warned the UK of “consequences” for providing long-range missile components to Ukraine, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that these “consequences” could include the possibility of attacks. He said many military experts advising the Kremlin are convinced that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.

This week, Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said he was unhappy to see Moscow represented at the G20 meeting on Monday. “We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” ⁠⁠he told Reuters.

On Tuesday, European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis also said this is not the right moment to “normalise” Moscow’s participation in G20 gatherings. “I think the European position is known,” Dombrovskis told reporters on the sidelines of the North Carolina meeting.

articles.title: MPSC drug inspector exam paper leak: ‘Top ranker’ Rutuja Patil arrested, intentionally gave 10 wrong answers
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police on Tuesday arrested a candidate who secured the seventh rank in the Maharashtra Public Service Commission’s (MPSC) Drug Inspecto.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police on Tuesday arrested a candidate who secured the seventh rank in the Maharashtra Public Service Commission’s (MPSC) Drug Inspector (Group-B) examination in connection with the alleged question paper leak, taking the total number of arrests in the case to seven.Rutuja Patil was arrested by the Mumbai Crime Branch’s Property Cell from Nandurbar, officials said, news agency PTI reported.Police alleged that Patil had received the leaked question paper before the examination. She was allegedly advised to deliberately answer 10 questions incorrectly to avoid raising suspicion.Patil was subsequently produced before a court and remanded to the custody of the Mumbai Crime Branch, officials said.Her arrest comes days after the Crime Branch arrested six persons, including three MPSC officials, in connection with the alleged leak of the question paper for the Drug Inspector (Group-B) screening examination conducted on March 22.The other accused have been identified as MPSC assistant section officers Vishweshwar Dattatraya Nakate and Gopal Bhattu Marathe, MPSC under secretary Abhijit Ganpatrao Lendwe, Kautilya Academy director Pravin Dilip Patil, and alleged co-conspirators Amrut Namdeo Patil and Lokesh alias Gaurav Rajendra Patil.According to the Crime Branch, the accused allegedly accessed the examination questions before the test, compiled them into a separate set and distributed them among unauthorised persons, PTI reported.The examination was conducted for recruitment to Drug Inspector (Group-B) posts under the Maharashtra food and drug administration department.Following a preliminary inquiry that found a breach in the confidentiality of the examination process, the MPSC cancelled the recruitment process and announced that a fresh examination would be conducted.The commission said the decision was taken to ensure a fair and equal opportunity for all candidates and to safeguard the integrity, transparency and impartiality of its examinations.The screening examination was held offline at six divisional headquarters across Maharashtra on March 22.The results were declared on June 12, after which 506 candidates were found eligible for the interview stage. Of these, 488 candidates appeared for interviews held between July 1 and 22.The MPSC later published a provisional general merit list of 488 candidates, including 485 who were found eligible for appointment.However, complaints alleging irregularities in the screening examination were received between July 22 and 26 from candidates and public representatives.The complaints alleged that some candidates had received the question paper, or questions from it, before the examination and that the material had subsequently been circulated through electronic platforms.The case has been registered under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Maharashtra Prevention of Malpractices at Competitive Examinations Act and the Prevention of Corruption Act.The charges include cheating, criminal breach of trust, criminal conspiracy and corruption by public servants.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: St Paul's Cathedral to host gigs in four-year Fabric deal
articles.summary: The cathedral has signed a deal with its exclusive contemporary music partner until 2030.
articles.body:
St Paul's Cathedral has signed a four-year deal with the London nightclub Fabric to stage music events inside the building.

Under the partnership, Fabric will be the cathedral's exclusive partner for such events until 2030. The first concert is due to take place on 29 October, although the artist has not been announced.

Fabric co-founder Cameron Leslie called the deal "an extraordinary and unexpected coming together of two very different parts of London".

Sandra Lynes Timbrell, the cathedral's director of visitor engagement, said she hoped a "carefully curated programme of exceptional concerts" would draw people who had not visited before.

"These events showcase world-class talent and create unforgettable experiences for audiences within one of London's most iconic spaces," she said.

She added that the cathedral wanted to encourage people "to discover and engage with this historic building in new and exciting ways".

Mr Leslie said Fabric had "always been about bringing people together through music", and that the club was looking to create "something genuinely special and befitting of this incredible space".

The organisers said the programme would feature artists "from different musical backgrounds and disciplines whose work responds to the Cathedral's distinctive atmosphere, acoustics and architectural heritage".

St Paul's has previously held concerts by the artists RY X in 2024 and Patti Smith in 2025.

Music events in cathedrals have proved contentious elsewhere.

Silent discos held at Canterbury Cathedral in 2024 were dubbed a "rave in the nave" by critics, and a petition calling for them to be stopped attracted more than 1,600 signatures.

Its organiser, Cajetan Skowronski, said at the time that such events would "not bring young people closer to Christ" and would instead suggest "that entertainment deserves our attention more than God".

Fabric, in Farringdon, had its licence revoked in 2016 after Islington Council found what it described as a culture of drug use at the venue.

Two 18-year-olds had died earlier that year in separate incidents after taking drugs at the club.

The venue reopened in January 2017 after agreeing new licensing conditions with the council and the Metropolitan Police, including a higher minimum entry age and tighter security.

articles.title: In 1944, Polish priest Henry Denis endured Nazi malaria experiments at Dachau; after surviving the camp, he fulfilled his vow by building Our Lady of Fatima Shrine in Nebraska
articles.summary: US News: A small roadside monument beside US Highway 34 in rural Nebraska carries the memory of a survival story that began inside the barracks of Dachau conce.
articles.body: A small roadside monument beside US Highway 34 in rural Nebraska carries the memory of a survival story that began inside the barracks of Dachau concentration camp. The Our Lady of Fatima Shrine, located on the grounds of St. Germanus Catholic Church in Arapahoe, was built to fulfil a solemn promise made by Father Henry J. Denis. Imprisoned by Nazi forces during the Second World War and subjected to deadly medical experiments, the Polish military chaplain vowed that if he survived the concentration camp, he would build a public shrine dedicated to the Blessed Mother. Details documented by Visit Nebraska and published by the Catholic Diocese of Lincoln describe how the priest survived years of imprisonment, medical experiments and near-fatal roll calls before moving to the United States and building the monument.Wartime arrest and the horrors of DachauBorn in Poland and ordained in 1936, Father Denis was serving as a chaplain in the Polish Army when Nazi forces invaded in September 1939. German troops arrested him soon after the invasion, beginning a series of transfers through concentration camps, including Buchenwald, before he was sent to Dachau in 1942. Historians and diocesan records say Dachau became the main camp for Christian clergy. Of the 1,773 Polish priests sent there, fewer than half survived. Clergy were banned from holding religious services, celebrating Mass or carrying religious items, with violations punishable by death. In a 1971 interview preserved by the Diocese of Lincoln, Father Denis described the strict rules imposed on priests: "For us, the offering of the Mass, confessions and reciting the rosary – all this was prohibited under the penalty of death. Two Austrian priests were caught praying the rosary, they were killed on the spot." To continue praying, Father Denis counted his prayers silently on his fingers while carrying out forced labour.Medical experiments and the call to roll callConditions became even worse in 1944 when Nazi doctors chose Father Denis for medical experiments on prisoners. For five months, doctors repeatedly infected him with malaria as part of research into tropical diseases. Many prisoners subjected to the same experiments died from the disease or from later lethal injections. Father Denis watched fellow prisoners die as the experiments continued. The key moment came on 7 October 1944, during the Feast of the Holy Rosary. Rain and cold winds swept through the camp as SS guards held a long morning roll call, shouting at and beating prisoners while checking every inmate. Recalling that morning in memoirs kept by the shrine, Father Denis wrote: "It was a cold, windy and rainy morning. There was a long, long roll call and prolonged counting. There were many corpses on that day, and all the dead had to be brought and placed in line with those who were alive. There was a lot of shouting, cursing, kicking and clubbing."While marching to his work detail, a fellow German priest asked Father Denis why camp commanders had called his name and identification number over the loudspeakers. Failing to report when called meant certain death. "My blood stopped to circulate," Father Denis recalled. "To be called and not to report at once – that's death, and death flashed in my mind as never before. Oh, what excruciating hours." When the workers returned to the camp that evening, guards did not look for him or call his number again. Instead, another priest prisoner, Father Francis Dachtera, reported to the SS block in his place and never returned. Realising that he had survived because of an error or unusual circumstance, Father Denis promised to build a shrine to Mary if he lived to see liberation.Freedom and the journey to NebraskaAmerican forces liberated Dachau on 29 April 1945. Weak from malaria and starvation, Father Denis spent months recovering in Europe. While recovering in Italy, he began sharing religious images of Our Lady of Częstochowa. This eventually brought him into contact with officials from the Diocese of Lincoln in Nebraska, who were looking for priests to serve rural parishes. Father Denis moved to the United States and served several small Nebraska communities before becoming pastor of St. Germanus Church in Arapahoe in 1949. After arriving in Furnas County, Father Denis first focused on his parish before raising money for the promise he had made during the war. To build the monument, he sought help from across North America and Europe, receiving building materials, stones and financial support from 43 American states, Canada and European donors.Construction of the roadside sanctuaryDedicated in August 1956, the Our Lady of Fatima Shrine recreates the 1917 Marian apparitions reported in Fatima, Portugal. The open-air site has a central, life-sized statue of Our Lady of Fatima with her head bowed and hands folded. It is flanked by statues of the three shepherd children, Lucia, Francisco and Jacinta, along with sculpted farm animals. An altar in front of the main statue carries an inscription explaining the site's history and purpose: "TO THE IMMACULATE MOTHER OF GOD AND OUR HEAVENLY FATHER / OUR LADY OF FATIMA / WITH HOPE AND PRAYER FOR PEACE / REV. HENRY J. DENIS AND HIS FRIENDS OF ALL FAITHS / 1956 / E PLURIBUS UNUM". Stone angels holding trumpets stand beside the altar, symbolising freedom and remembering those who died in wartime atrocities. Walking paths around the shrine were later expanded to include a Rosary Walk through native landscaping beside the historic 1885 wooden parish church. The shrine remains open to travellers, pilgrims and local visitors, serving as a quiet reminder of survival and a promise kept across two continents.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: A forensic team from India has begun analysing DNA samples in Nepal, as rescue teams continue the search for people missing after catastrophic flash floods swept through the Himalayan region on August 26.In an X post, India In Nepal wrote, "The 19-member Indian Forensic Team began DNA sample analysis in collaboration with their Nepali counterparts at the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory and the National Forensic Science Laboratory, Khumaltar, Kathmandu."The Embassy of India said the team was working to expedite DNA sample processing to help identify people affected by the floods. articles.title: Jerusalem schools strike after Israel enforces curriculum and bans teachers
articles.summary: East Jerusalem schools strike as Israeli permit bans and forced curricula plunge the academic year into chaos.
articles.body:
The academic year in occupied East Jerusalem began on Tuesday with an open-ended strike by teachers at private and Christian schools after Israeli meddling in students’ curriculum.

All new first and seventh-grade classes at East Jerusalem’s Palestinian-majority municipal schools have been told to exclusively use the Israeli curriculum this year.

Entry permits for West Bank teachers to teach in East Jerusalem schools have also been blocked by Israel, according to Haaretz.

It means that one-in-three Palestinian students in occupied East Jerusalem, more than 45,000 in total, will be enrolled in the Israeli educational programme, a nearly fourfold increase over six years ago.

Jerusalem Governorate spokesman Marouf al-Rifai described the forced integration of Israeli curriculum into Palestinian schools as a cultural and educational crime.

“The adherence of Jerusalem’s people, teachers, and students to the Palestinian curriculum is not merely an adherence to a textbook, but rather a defense of memory, identity, history, and the right to determine the national narrative,” he said in a statement on Facebook.

Israeli forces recently seized educational compounds formerly operated by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, in the Shu’fat refugee camp and Kafr Aqab, to be replaced with Israeli-administered facilities.

Hamas official Haroun Nasser el-Din issued a statement saying that “the school, the book, and awareness are basic pillars in the battle of Jerusalem”. East Jerusalem and the West Bank have been illegally occupied by Israel since 1967.

“The Palestinian identity in Jerusalem is deeper than to be erased by imposed curricula or the occupation’s procedures and its arrogant policies,” he added.

Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem have already suffered a severe staffing shortage due to Israel effectively blocking teachers from the West Bank from reaching the city’s schools. The General Secretariat for Christian Educational Institutions in Jerusalem announced an indefinite strike in response to the crisis.

“We were surprised, unfortunately once again, by the non-renewal of entry permits for more than 70 teachers and employees from our educational, administrative, and support cadres, in a sudden manner and without prior warning, which hindered their access to their schools and directly affected their readiness for the opening of the school year,” the body said in a statement.

“The absence of this large number of cadres affects various aspects of school work, educational, administrative, and health, in addition to cleaning services and security and safety procedures, which makes it impossible to guarantee a safe and stable start for our students.”

Sylvia Amer, deputy director for academic and administrative affairs at College des Freres Jerusalem, said that the abrupt reversal of dozens of permits just 10 days before schools were due to open forced the suspension of classes.

“The sudden ban came after they had previously confirmed to us in June that all permits would be available for all members of our teaching and administrative staff and employees,” Amer said.

“If this reality continues, it will gradually lead to affecting the independence of schools and their educational and cultural identity”.

The staffing crisis at East Jerusalem schools has been worsened by recent Israeli legislation targeting Palestinian schools.

A Knesset law passed earlier this year prohibits the employment of teachers holding academic degrees from Palestinian Authority institutions within the Israeli educational system.

This effectively targets the core of East Jerusalem’s teaching workforce, where approximately 60 percent of the 6,700 Arab educators hold Palestinian degrees, according to the Haaretz report.

Mike Bassam Farraj, general director of Greek Orthodox Patriarchate Schools, told Al Jazeera that the permit denials and legislative hurdles act as a systematic pressure campaign.

“It serves as a systematic pressure method practised on Christian schools in Jerusalem and private schools in general, aiming to reduce the numbers of employees and teachers coming from the West Bank,” Farraj noted.

Israeli authorities have also weaponised budgetary allocations to coerce institutions, he added.

“In reality, there are continuous financial temptations – so as not to use the word ‘blackmail’ – based on the equation: ‘Adopt the Israeli Bagrut curriculum and take whatever budgets you wish,’ where they then grant you much broader spaces and capabilities,” Farraj explained.

To counter this academic siege, Farraj detailed their reliance on the judiciary.

“As for some other professions, we are forced to engage in legal confrontations and relentless follow-ups before responsible and governmental authorities,” he explained.

“The matter often reaches – as in the specialisation of human medicine, for example – obtaining decisions from the Supreme Court to extract and prove the right of our graduates to obtain professional practice certificates according to their specialisations, whether in medicine or law or others.”

articles.title: Qatar says efforts under way to end Iran-US war and reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Qatar accuses Israel of exploiting regional conflicts to impose new realities in Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria.
articles.body:
Qatar is holding talks with Oman and Pakistan to de-escalate tensions in the region, the country’s Foreign Ministry has said, after a recent flare-up in fighting between the US and Iran.

Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari warned on Tuesday against normalising the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war between Iran and the US has seen shipping in the waterway grind almost to a halt.

“We said from the start, any attempt to normalise the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in this way will end with regional escalation, and this is what we saw yesterday and today,” Al-Ansari said in the press conference.

“Escalation does not benefit anyone, and we are all negatively impacted by the escalation. We encourage all sides to be wise and return to negotiations.”

Around 25 percent of the world’s seaborne trade passed through the strait before Israel and the US launched a war on Iran on February 28, reducing traffic in the waterway to a trickle.

The US has enforced a blockade on Iranian ports, while Iran has been accused of laying mines and attacking tankers in the waterway. Energy prices have since skyrocketed, affecting economies across the world.

Iran and Oman have held talks on opening a temporary route through the Strait of Hormuz, but Tehran wants the US to first return to a memorandum of understanding agreed in June.

Qatar, which has been economically impacted by the war, has encouraged a peaceful resolution to the crisis and is in contact with regional leaders to encourage dialogue, Al-Ansari said.

Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani visited Tehran last week to encourage dialogue to end the crisis.

“The [regional] visits [to Tehran]… are all to support mediation efforts, and attempting to return to the negotiation path, and guaranteeing no return to escalation in the region,” Al-Ansari said about the visit.

“During his visit [the Qatari Prime Minister] confirmed Qatar’s consistent position in support of diplomatic efforts to find a solution to this crisis… efforts are ongoing.”

While the US and Iran battle over the waterway, Israel has continued to bomb and occupy Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.

Recent weeks have also seen a spike in pogroms by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, with Palestinian homes and villages besieged.

Al-Ansari accused Israel of using the war on Iran “to impose a new reality in Palestinian, Lebanese and Syrian territories” and accused it of beginning a new regional escalation.

articles.summary: The Hindu rituals of death, cremation, prayer and final farewell have been overwhelmed by the scale of the disaster.
articles.body:
Nepal has begun burying the victims of the devastating flood that hit the mountainous country last week in mass graves after taking DNA samples.

Nepal has begun burying victims of last week’s devastating flood in mass graves after taking DNA samples.

Nepalese authorities said on Tuesday that 1,003 bodies had been recovered, with 3,916 people still listed as missing, following the massive surge of freezing water, rocks and debris that tore down Himalayan valleys on August 26.

The deadly wave was triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse, and then carved a path of destruction through the country.

At a mass burial ground in Chitwan district, the Hindu rituals of death, cremation, prayer and final farewell have been overwhelmed by the scale of the disaster, as authorities bury unidentified bodies after DNA sampling because there are too many to store or identify individually.

Police using a drone to search for survivors said on Tuesday they had found 24 bodies in a single house in Nuwakot district. At least 17 bodies have been recovered from rivers far downstream in India.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah has described the catastrophe as “unimaginable and heartbreaking”.
