articles.title: U.N. World Food Programme slashes West Bank aid,  Gaza faces new cuts
articles.summary: The United Nations’ food agency said it is halving food assistance in the Israeli-occupied West Bank because of severe funding shortages.
articles.body: The United Nations’ food agency said Tuesday it is halving food assistance in the Israeli-occupied West Bank because of severe funding shortages and warned it may be forced to make further cuts in Gaza, where it supports 1.5 million people. The U.N. World Food Programme said it will reduce assistance in the West Bank from 400,000 people to 200,000 beginning this month. In Gaza, it reduced the value of cash assistance by 40% for 375,000 people in July and said additional cuts will be unavoidable unless it secures new funding. WFP said it urgently needs an additional $386 million over the next six months to assist an estimated 2 million food-insecure people across Gaza and the West Bank. The world’s leading authority on food insecurity, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, said in July the situation in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in parts of the Palestinian territory last year, but warned conditions were still at crisis levels. Also in July, the WFP cautioned that funding shortages and what it described as donor fatigue could force deeper reductions in Gaza and said it needed more than $420 million to sustain operations in Gaza and the West Bank through the end of the year. In the West Bank, WFP estimated in its Tuesday report that 900,000 people are food insecure. The agency said increased violence, displacement and economic deterioration have disrupted livelihoods and deepened hunger, while food needs have more than doubled since 2023. “Families who were once thriving and earning a living from their land are now unable to afford enough food,” Shaun Hughes, WFP’s country director, said in a statement Tuesday. He added the agency was being forced to prioritize the most vulnerable households while cutting assistance to others despite widespread need. According to WFP’s latest food security analysis, 76% of households in the West Bank have experienced a significant decline in income. One-third cannot afford a nutritious diet, while food and fuel prices remain among the highest in the Middle East. Rural communities and the southern West Bank are among the hardest hit, the agency said. Humanitarian conditions also remain severe in Gaza. According to recent U.N. figures from aid agencies, about one in five families ate only one meal a day, while half reported running out of food entirely at least once in the previous month. Aid agencies say cash shortages and soaring food prices have made it increasingly difficult for families to obtain basic necessities. According to WFP, three-quarters of households in Gaza had difficulty accessing markets in August. The U.N. and its partners recently collected hundreds of pallets of food, fuel and other supplies through the Kerem Shalom crossing and distributed food parcels and wheat flour to more than 600,000 people during the August aid cycle. Despite a ceasefire signed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025, ongoing hostilities and security restrictions continue to hamper movement and recovery efforts, according to U.N. agencies. The U.N. says more than 2 million people have been displaced during the war and that much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure, including homes, hospitals, schools and water facilities, has been damaged or destroyed.

articles.title: Nigeria's EFCC chief has fired 40 of his anti-corruption agents for 'being corrupt'
articles.summary: The EFCC boss says more than five of the dismissed officials are already facing prosecution.
articles.body:
Nigeria's anti-corruption agency has dismissed more than 40 employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years.

The disclosure was made by Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) chairman Ola Olukoyede at an event assessing the agency's achievements since he took the helm in October 2023.

He said more than five of the dismissed officials were already facing prosecution, while case files are being prepared against others.

The EFCC investigates financial crimes, including fraud, money laundering and corruption - regularly pursuing cases against politicians, public officials, business figures and others accused of misusing public funds.

"In the past two-and-a-half years or three years of my service, I've asked them to dismiss over 40 staff on account of corruption and financial malpractice," Olukoyede told journalists at the briefing in the capital, Abuja.

He went on to explain that as part of the reforms he had overseen at the agency, the EFCC's Department of Internal Affairs had been renamed "the Department of Ethics and Integrity".

To fight against conflicts of interest, a policy on gifts and hospitality had also been introduced.

It requires officers to declare gifts above a certain threshold - which he did not specify - including gifts received from relatives abroad.

"You must be sure that your hands are clean. You can't be fighting corruption when your hands are soiled with corrupt practices," Olukoyede said.

The BBC asked the EFCC for more details about the alleged corruption involving its former staff members, but the agency said this information was not available.

It was keen to point to its other achievements over the last three years - highlighted at Monday's briefing .

Olukoyede, 56, said he had overseen a record-breaking time for the EFCC, recovering 1.23 trillion naira ($925m, £683m), with a conviction rate of more than 75%.

"The commission received 49,673 petitions, investigated 39,615 cases, filed 14,476 cases in court and secured 10,872 convictions between October 2023 and July 2026," he said.

In the first half of 2026 alone, it had recorded 1,370 convictions from 1,889 filings, the EFCC chairman added.

"These results reflect diligence, resilience and a prosecutorial approach anchored on evidence and courtroom outcomes."

Other figures disclosed at the event show that the EFCC's caseload is increasingly focused on cybercrime and fraud rather than just corruption cases against high-profile officials.

articles.title: Grangetown house fire victim, 7, was 'deeply loved'
articles.summary: Valentina Foster's parents say their lives were changed forever by her "devastating loss".
articles.body:
The family of a seven-year-old girl killed in a house fire said their lives had been changed forever by her "devastating loss".

Valentina Foster died alongside her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, in the blaze at Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August. A man has been charged with their murders.

In a tribute, the youngster's parents said their daughter would "always be in our hearts, and her memory will live with us forever".

"She was deeply loved and will be missed beyond words by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched," they said.

"Our lives have changed forever, and we are struggling to come to terms with this devastating loss."

They added she would be "forever missed" by her brothers and sisters.

On Tuesday, Jaden Wright, 23, appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with two counts of murder as well as multiple grievous bodily harm offences in connection with the blaze.

A 31-year-old man arrested on suspicion of murder was released with no further action.

Cleveland Police said a man and a woman remained in hospital while two teenage girls were discharged following treatment.

Lisa Kirton, Natalie's mother, previously told the BBC her daughter was "lovely, bright and bubbly" and "everybody loved her".

Initially police said they could not exclude a connection between the fire and organised crime linked to seven deaths, including two police officers, in a crash on the A66 .

It since said the cases were not linked.

articles.title: Port Talbot paedophile who abused children jailed for 21 years
articles.summary: Craig Henton told online users he had befriended a vulnerable mother to gain access to her daughter.
articles.body:
A predatory and dangerous paedophile who abused a young child and used chatrooms to plan the abuse of others has been jailed for 21 years.

Craig Henton, 54, was tracked down from an encrypted messaging app where he had said he had planned to commit sexual offences against a five-year-old girl.

Investigators found more than 4,000 indecent images and videos at Henton's home in Port Talbot.

He admitted 18 offences in October 2025, ahead of his sentencing at Swansea Crown Court on Tuesday.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) said Henton was a "predatory and dangerous paedophile" who had abused a child and had shown "willingness to meet up with others... to satisfy his depraved sexual gratification".

The NCA, which led the investigation, said Henton had told app users between February and May 2024 that he had been a paedophile for 25 years.

He had said he had befriended a vulnerable mother to gain access to her daughter and groom her with the intention of sexually abusing her.

His phone had showed he had participated in hundreds of chats with users about the sexual abuse of children and discussed meeting up with them and their children so he could commit abuse.

During the NCA investigation, a total of 4,570 indecent images and videos were found on a device seized from Henton, including 918 in category A, the most serious type.

The NCA said the child that Henton said he had sexually assaulted, who was aged between three and five, had been identified and safeguarded.

Henton was arrested again in May and June 2024 on suspicion of assault of a girl under 13 and arranging the commission of a child sex offence, according to the UK's law enforcement agency.

When questioned by investigators, Henton made no comment, but was charged with 18 offences.

The NCA said further indecent images of children had been recovered from another device that had been seized from Henton in April 2024, totalling almost 1,400 images.

In addition to his sentence of 21 years in prison, Henton was given a further six years on licence and an indefinite sexual harm prevention order.

Henton will be on the sex offender register for life, and his victims were granted indefinite restraining orders against him.

Danielle Pownall, from the NCA, said Henton "joined chat groups set up purely to enable and justify the sexual abuse of children".

"He was open about being a paedophile for 25 years and his intention to target vulnerable women so he could abuse their children," she said.

"The NCA will continue in our work with partners in the UK and internationally to protect children from vile abusers like Henton."

articles.title: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but  judge asks them to keep trying
articles.summary: The Massachusetts mother is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.
articles.body:
Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after three days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.

Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.

Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed her children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and therefore could not distinguish right from wrong.

The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them.

The jury, comprised of nine women and three men, began its deliberations last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses.

On Tuesday, as Judge William Sullivan read out the jury's note, audible gasps of shock could be heard in the room. Clancy appeared stoic, sitting in a wheelchair next to her attorney.

It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations.

A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC.

"If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said.

But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said.

If found guilty, Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole.
